review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The global burden of microbial infections and antimicrobial resistance, coupled with the absence of
precise bacterial recognition modalities, demands innovative breakthroughs in antibacterial treatment.
Here, we report a chirality-specific biomimic—D-alanine-conjugated peptidoglycan mimics (D-PM)—
designed for bacterial recognition. D-PM exhibit broad-spectrum, effective recognition across ESKAPE
pathogens, antibiotic-resistant strains and clinical isolates, while displaying minimal interaction with
eukaryotic cells. We elucidate the bacterial recognition mechanism, wherein D-PM—act as biosynthetic
substrates—become incorporated into peptidoglycan biosynthesis. This reveals a mechanism by which
macromolecular mimetics are assimilated into bacterial biosynthesis, providing insights into bacterial
recognition. Beyond recognition, D-PM enable the construction of pathogen-specific imaging agents and
antibiotic-targeted delivery systems. In localized and systemic infection models, D-PM achieve efficient
pathogen localization, tissue penetration, and enhanced therapeutic outcomes. This work presents a
molecularly engineered strategy for bacterial recognition and intervention, offering a translational
approach to address the escalating threat of infectious diseases.

---

## Introduction

Microbial infections continue to pose a formidable threat to human health, accounting for more than 7
million deaths annually1,2. This escalating crisis highlights an urgent need for effective approaches that
enable the precise diagnosis and targeted intervention of pathogenic infections3,4. Central to this
challenge is the accurate recognition of bacterial pathogens—an indispensable prerequisite for effective
treatment and resistance mitigation5,6. Despite significant advances in bacterial recognition,
differentiating pathogenic bacteria from host components within complex biological environments
remains profoundly difficult, posing a major obstacle to clinical antibacterial therapy7,8. As a result, the
development of robust strategies for bacterial recognition has emerged as a critical scientific imperative
in the global battle against infectious diseases.

The bacterial cell wall, built upon a peptidoglycan scaffold, constitutes one of the most fundamental
distinctions between prokaryotic pathogens and eukaryotic hosts9. Peptidoglycan—universally composed
of sugar moieties and chirality-specific amino acids—is highly conserved across bacterial taxa
(Supplementary Fig. 1)10-13, which presents unique molecular signatures for precise bacterial recognition14-
18. Although peptidoglycan-targeting antibiotics—such as vancomycin—have served as pivotal agents for
bacterial eradication and detection19-23, their efficacy is increasingly compromised by target mutations
and emerging resistance24-26. Concurrently, increasing efforts have been directed toward biosynthetic
labeling for bacterial recognition, drawing inspiration from the bacterial-specific sugars (e.g., N-
acetylglucosamine, N-acetylmuramic acid) and amino acids (e.g., D-alanine) essential for peptidoglycan
biosynthesis27-32. However, these small-molecule probes are intrinsically constrained by limited structural
tunability, suboptimal recognition efficiency, and restricted biological permeability33,34. These persistent
limitations necessitate bacterial recognition platforms that break through conventional intervention
paradigms and molecular designs.

Emerging evidence suggests that macromolecular analogues of bacterial peptidoglycan, endowed
with superior biomimetic properties, represent promising candidates for targeted bacterial intervention35.
For instance, chitin—a natural polysaccharide sharing partial structural features with peptidoglycan—
exhibits comparable recognition by host pattern recognition receptors36,37, while synthetic
glycoconjugates have been shown to elicit peptidoglycan-mimetic immune responses38,39. Inspired by
these findings, we rationally designed macromolecular mimics of peptidoglycan substrates that
recapitulate the chirality-specific amino acid motifs and glycan backbone architectures (Supplementary
Fig. 2). In this work, we delineate the design principles of peptidoglycan mimics, elucidate their structure–
function relationships and biological mechanisms of bacterial biosynthetic incorporation (Fig. 1a and
Supplementary Fig. 3), and demonstrate their capability to selectively distinguish pathogenic bacteria
from host cells. Furthermore, we engineered these peptidoglycan mimics into nanoparticulate probes and
antibiotic delivery platforms, enabling targeted intervention of bacterial infections. This multidisciplinary
study establishes a transformative solution for bacterial diagnostics and therapeutics, providing effective
strategies to tackle the global burden of resistant microbial infections.

---

## Results

Chiral peptidoglycan mimics label bacteria
To enable the controlled synthesis of chiral peptidoglycan mimics (PM), protected chiral alanine (Ala) was
conjugated to glucosamine (GlcNH ) in chitosans (CS, (GlcN)ₙ analogous to the polysaccharide chain of
2
peptidoglycan) via amide bond formation under racemization-free conditions40,41. A series of chiral amino
acid-conjugated (GlcN) polymers was synthesized with varying degrees of L-Ala (7.5 ± 0.3%, 11.3 ± 0.4%,
n
17.7 ± 0.3%, and 23.5 ± 0.4%) or D-Ala (7.4 ± 0.6%, 11.6 ± 0.4%, 17.2 ± 0.3%, and 22.9 ± 0.8%) modification,
respectively (Supplementary Fig. 4). Following deprotection, L-PM of (GlcN–L-Ala) and D-PM of (GlcN–D-
n
Ala) were obtained with distinct Ala modification but identical fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) labeling.
n

The bacterial interactions of the chiral PM were quantified using Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus
ATCC29213) as a model strain. L-PM exhibited consistently low binding efficiency with minimal
dependence on the modification ratio, yielding FITC-positive bacterial populations ranging from 2.9 ± 0.2%
to 14.1 ± 0.4% (Supplementary Fig. 5). In contrast, D-PM displayed a pronounced modification-ratio-
dependent recognition behavior, with the proportion of FITC-positive bacteria increasing from 27.3 ± 2.7%
to 94.1 ± 0.3%. Notably, maximal bacterial labeling was achieved at a D-Ala modification degree of 17.2%,
whereas further increasing the substitution to 22.9% resulted in diminished labeling efficiency, likely due
to steric congestion that impairs enzymatic incorporation during cell wall biosynthesis. On this basis, the
17.2% modification rate of D-PM was selected for all subsequent studies. 1H nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR) spectra confirmed the successful conjugation of chiral amino acids onto (GlcN) , as evidenced by
n
the concurrent appearance of characteristic signals corresponding to sugar rings and amino acids
(Supplementary Fig. 6). Both L-PM and D-PM exhibited zeta potentials comparable to that of native CS
(approximately +23 mV) in aqueous solution (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Dynamic light scattering (DLS)
analysis indicated that CS could form aggregates around 350 nm in an aqueous solution, whereas both L-
PM and D-PM assembled into smaller nanostructures of 160 nm (Supplementary Fig. 7b-d). Transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) revealed well-defined nanostructures of both L-PM and D-PM, highlighting
their potential as functional nanomaterials. The circular dichroism spectra revealed distinct trends, with
L-PM showing a more pronounced attenuation of the negative band at 212 nm, but D-PM exhibiting a
greater increase in the positive band at 193 nm (Supplementary Fig. 8). These spectral variations are likely
attributed to the modifications induced by the chiral amino acids.

Chiral peptidoglycan mimics with abundant free amino groups facilitated effortless conjugation with
diverse fluorescent molecules, including FITC, 6-carboxytetramethylrhodamine (TAMRA), and sulfo-
cyanine5 (Cy5), facilitating sophisticated biological imaging (Supplementary Fig. 9). Moreover, both L-PM
and D-PM enhanced the stability of the fluorescent probes, with no detectable fluorescence decay over
10 days (Supplementary Fig. 10). To assess bacterial labeling performance, FITC-labeled CS, L-PM, and D-
PM were applied at identical concentrations and normalized to equivalent fluorescence intensities
(Supplementary Fig. 11). Strikingly, flow cytometric analysis revealed that D-PM displayed high-affinity
interactions across a broad panel of Gram-positive pathogenic bacteria42, including multiple
Staphylococcus aureus strains (S. aureus ATCC29213, S. aureus ATCC25904, and S. aureus RN4220), two
Enterococcus faecalis strains (E. faecalis ATCC29212 and E. faecalis ATCC19433), methicillin-resistant
Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA ATCC43300), as well as clinically isolated Staphylococcus aureus (Fig. 1b and
Supplementary Fig. 12). Meanwhile, D-PM also demonstrated significantly stronger recognition and
binding toward Gram-negative ESKAPE pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae
ATCC13883), Acinetobacter baumannii (A. baumannii ATCC19606), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P.
aeruginosa ATCC27853), and Escherichia coli (E. coli ATCC25922), compared with CS and L-PM
(Supplementary Fig. 13). In addition, the relatively lower labeling efficiency observed for certain Gram-
negative species in the D-PM-treated group, including K. pneumoniae and E. coli, is likely attributable to
the presence of an outer membrane that partially restricts D-PM access to the peptidoglycan43. By
contrast, both CS and L-PM exhibited uniformly low binding efficacy toward both Gram-positive and
Gram-negative bacterial strains. More importantly, D-PM exhibited robust bacterial binding and
fluorescent labeling as visualized by confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM), clearly delineating the
coccoid morphology of S. aureus ATCC29213 (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 14). D-PM exhibited
pronounced dose-dependent binding to bacteria, indicative of its potential accumulation on the bacteria
(Supplementary Fig. 15). Taken together, D-PM exhibit chirality-dependent biological effects that enable
broad-spectrum and highly efficient recognition of pathogenic bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant
strains.

To investigate the bacterial recognition advantage conferred by chiral peptidoglycan mimic design,
we compared FITC-labeled D-PM with FITC-labeled small-molecule D-Ala probes at matched D-Ala molar
equivalents. Two control conditions were employed: (1) a D-Ala/FITC-labeled D-Ala mixture calibrated to
match the fluorescence intensity of FITC-labeled D-PM, and (2) fully FITC-labeled D-Ala with substantially
higher overall fluorescence than FITC-labeled D-PM (Supplementary Fig. 16). Under fluorescence-matched
conditions of probe, only 2.6 ± 0.2% of bacteria were FITC-positive following treatment with the D-
Ala/FITC-labeled D-Ala mixture, which was dramatically lower than the 85.7 ± 0.2% FITC-positive bacteria
observed in the FITC-labeled D-PM group. The mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) in the FITC-labeled D-
PM-treated bacteria was about 8-fold higher than that of the D-Ala/FITC-labeled D-Ala mixture. Notably,
even compared with fully FITC-labeled D-Ala with approximately 4-fold higher fluorescence than FITC-
labeled D-PM, both the proportion of FITC-positive bacteria and MFI remained higher in the FITC-labeled
D-PM-treated group. CLSM images clearly demonstrate the overwhelming performance of D-PM in
bacterial fluorescent labeling (Supplementary Fig. 17). These results underscore the superior bacterial
recognition efficiency afforded by D-chiral peptidoglycan mimics, highlighting the intrinsic advantages of
chirality-guided macromolecular design over small-molecule D-Ala–based probes for pathogenic bacteria.

D-PM incorporate biosynthetic downstream
To elucidate the recognition mechanisms, microscale thermophoresis (MST) was employed to generate
binding curves that characterized the interactions between chiral peptidoglycan mimics and S. aureus44.
The results revealed a significant interaction between D-PM and bacteria, with a dissociation constant (K )
d
of 5.4 ± 0.3 μM—an order of magnitude lower than that of both CS and L-PM (Fig. 2a). This finding
indicated that the D-chiral strategy enhanced the affinity between D-PM and pathogenic bacteria (S.
aureus ATCC29213). In parallel, flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that FITC-labeled D-PM rapidly
bound to bacteria over time, achieving near-complete binding efficiency (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig.
18). The maximal binding rates of fluorescent CS and L-PM with bacteria remained below 20%.
These striking differences suggested that D-PM may engage distinct mechanisms in binding to bacteria,
potentially involving biosynthetic processes.

Uridine 5’-diphosphate-N-acetylmuramic acid pentapeptide (UDP-MurNAc pentapeptide) is a well-
established biomarker of cell wall synthesis intervention, whose accumulation is notably induced by
vancomycin (Van)23,45. An ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography system coupled with a high-
resolution quadrupole–orbitrap mass spectrometer (UPLC-MS) revealed the presence of a characteristic
peak for UDP-MurNAc pentapeptide at 1,150.3583 in the bacterial wall of S. aureus following exposure to
D-PM, consistent with the signal observed after vancomycin treatment (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig.
19). In contrast, UDP-MurNAc pentapeptide was undetectable in both the CS and L-PM groups. Moreover,
flow cytometry results indicated that pretreatment with vancomycin significantly reduced D-PM binding
to S. aureus, likely due to competitive interference in cell wall synthesis (Supplementary Fig. 20).
Inspection of UPLC-MS results revealed that D-peptidoglycan mimics interfered with the biosynthesis
of the bacterial cell wall. The observed peak at m/z 322.1613 was assigned to the protonated molecular
ion [GlcN–D-Ala–D-Ala + H]⁺ (theoretical m/z 322.1609), which likely arises from the ligation of an
additional D-Ala to the D-PM substrate (GlcN–D-Ala) catalyzed by D-Ala–D-Ala ligase (Ddl, Fig. 2d,e)27. This
intermediate, GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala, could subsequently be incorporated into the cell wall biosynthesis
pathway to form GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala-L-Lys-D-iGlu-L-Ala-MurNAc through the biocatalyst of UDP-N-
acetylmuramoyl-tripeptide–D-alanyl-D-Ala ligase (MurF), with a characteristic ion peak at m/z 925.4353
(Fig. 2f,g). To further elucidate the structural basis of D-PM interference in cell wall synthesis, we used the
catalytic domain of Ddl bound to GlcN-D-Ala and determined the structure of the complex. Docking
analysis revealed that D-PM, as a substrate bind to Ddl in a pocket highly analogous to that of D-Ala within
the overall complex structure (Fig. 2h,i and Supplementary Fig. 21a,b). Furthermore, the strong binding
affinity of D-PM to Ddl was further supported by a lower docking score of -6.775 kcal mol-1, compared to
the D-Ala/Ddl complex, which had a docking score of -4.077 kcal mol-1. Similarly, the intermediate of GlcN-
D-Ala-D-Ala exhibited a better docking score of -8.088 kcal mol-1 as compared to natural D-Ala-D-Ala
(docking score of -6.042 kcal mol-1) when bound to the catalytic pocket of MurF (Supplementary Fig. 21c,d).
Subsequently, molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the GlcN–D-Ala/Ddl and GlcN–D-Ala–D-
Ala/MurF complexes exhibited sustained structural stability, with markedly stronger interactions than
those observed between conventional small-molecule substrates (D-Ala or D-Ala–D-Ala) and their
corresponding ligases (Supplementary Figs. 22 and 23). UPLC-MS evidence and molecular simulations
jointly confirmed that chirality-specific peptidoglycan mimics could efficiently integrate into the
metabolism downstream of bacterial cell wall biosynthesis, thereby facilitating the robust recognition and
biosynthetic labeling of pathogens.

In addition, key cell wall synthesis inhibitors, including D-cycloserine (D-Ala-D-Ala ligase inhibitor),
amoxicillin and meropenem (penicillin-binding protein transpeptidase inhibitor)43, were able to block the
incorporation of D-PM into downstream metabolic pathways (Fig. 2j). In contrast, a protein synthesis
inhibitor of tetracycline and a DNA synthesis inhibitor of ciprofloxacin showed no effect on the
incorporation of D-PM into S. aureus. In addition, none of the inhibitors significantly affected the binding
of CS and L-PM to the bacteria (Supplementary Fig. 24). The chiral-specific design of D-peptidoglycan
mimics enables their integration into bacterial cell wall synthesis metabolism, thereby facilitating efficient
bacterial recognition and targeting.

Encouraged by the molecular-level confirmation of downstream metabolism, we proceeded to
investigate the impact of D-PM on the morphology of pathogenic bacteria. FITC-labeled peptidoglycan
mimics were incubated with S. aureus over three passages in Luria–Bertani broth (Fig. 3a). As shown in
Fig. 3b, only a small proportion of fluorescent L-PM bound to S. aureus ATCC29213, always with around
10% of bacteria exhibiting fluorescence. This minimal binding of L-PM is attributable to weak interactions
governed by a dynamic adsorption-desorption equilibrium, as evidenced by the reduced bacterial surface
zeta potential following supramolecular electrostatic interactions between L-PM and the bacterial
envelope (Supplementary Fig. 25). Under the same conditions, continuous co-incubation with D-PM from
Passage 1 to Passage 3 led to a progressive increase in the percentage of fluorescent bacteria, rising from
16.1% to 44.3%. This outcome was due to the incorporation of D-PM into bacterial metabolism, enabling
the accumulation over successive generations during bacterial proliferation. To visualize this generational
integration, super-resolution three-dimensional structured illumination microscopy (3D-SIM) provided
direct evidence of D-PM incorporation into bacterial cell wall synthesis (Fig. 3c,d). In Passage 1, Cy5-
labeled D-PM well-delineated the bacterial cell wall (red fluorescence). In Passage 2, TAMRA-labeled D-
PM was incorporated into the biosynthesis of bacterial envelopes (purple fluorescence), while Cy5-labeled
D-PM remained prominently visible on the bacteria. The approximately half reduction in Cy5 fluorescence
intensity was attributed to fluorescence dilution during bacterial division in Passage 2. In Passage 3, co-
incubation with FITC-labeled D-PM (green fluorescence) demonstrated clear co-localization of red, purple,
and green fluorescence along the bacterial contours, indicating stable incorporation of D-PM into the
downstream metabolism of cell wall synthesis. In contrast, L-PM showed minimal co-localization with
bacteria, consistent with flow cytometry results, and failed to accumulate within the bacterial cell wall.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of bacteria over three passages in the presence of L-PM
or D-PM revealed distinct morphological differences (Fig. 3e). In the L-PM-treated groups, bacteria
retained well-defined surfaces, appearing consistent with both the control and CS-treated groups.
However, D-PM induced notable structural abnormalities, characterized by visible protrusions on the
bacterial surface. These deformities are likely attributed to the incorporation of D-PM into cell wall
synthesis, disrupting the formation of a cohesive peptidoglycan network. Additionally, propidium iodide
(PI) probe assays confirmed the compromised bacterial envelope integrity after three passages in the
presence of D-PM (Fig. 3f). The PI influx in the D-PM-treated group was significantly higher than that
observed in the control and L-PM-treated groups, indicating abnormal envelopes. In addition, colony-
forming unit (CFU) assays demonstrated that incorporation of D-PM into bacterial cell wall biosynthesis
elicited a modest bactericidal effect at Passage 1 (Supplementary Fig. 26). With successive passages up to
Passage 3, progressive accumulation of D-PM within the peptidoglycan increasingly compromised cell wall
integrity, leading to a stepwise enhancement of bactericidal activity. These findings confirmed that D-PM
could be efficiently incorporated into bacterial cell wall biosynthesis and progressively accumulates within
the peptidoglycan.

D-PM recognize bacteria over mammalian cells
D-PM achieved efficient integration into bacterial biosynthesis, exhibiting satisfactory bacterial
recognition. By leveraging the intrinsic differences in chiral amino acid metabolism between prokaryotic
pathogens and mammalian cells, D-PM demonstrated significant potential for selectively distinguishing
these entities, paving the way for advancements in the diagnosis and treatment of bacterial infections. As
expected, CS, L-PM, and D-PM exhibited minimal interactions with animal cell lines at concentrations
corresponding to those used for bacterial incubation, including mouse NIH 3T3 cells, human umbilical vein
endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and monkey Vero cells (Supplementary Fig. 27). Additionally, MST
measurements revealed no detectable specific binding of CS, L-PM, or D-PM to NIH 3T3 cells
(Supplementary Fig. 28), and UPLC-MS analysis targeting characteristic peptidoglycan-derived motifs
detected no corresponding signals in NIH 3T3 cells following incubation with CS, L-PM, or D-PM
(Supplementary Fig. 29). Co-culture with prokaryotic bacteria and eukaryotic cells in the presence of
fluorescent D-PM revealed a clear preference for bacterial recognition by flow cytometry analysis (Fig. 4a).
As shown in Fig. 4b, D-PM selectively associated with S. aureus, with approximately 30% of bacteria
exhibiting FITC-positive fluorescence, whereas binding to mammalian NIH 3T3 cells was much lower.
Additionally, D-PM exhibited robust specificity for identifying S. aureus over a range of the mammalian
cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 30). CLSM images directly showed that demonstrated that D-PM (green)
exhibited strong co-localization with S. aureus but poor co-localization with NIH 3T3 cells, confirming the
remarkable selectivity of D-PM in distinguishing bacteria from mammalian cells (Fig. 4c). In addition, flow
cytometry and CLSM images revealed that CS and L-PM exhibited minimal binding to S. aureus and NIH
3T3 cells under co-culture conditions (Supplementary Figs. 31 and 32). Similarly, D-PM effectively
distinguished multiple Gram-negative bacterial species from NIH 3T3 cells under co-culture conditions
(Supplementary Fig. 33). These findings highlight the potential of D-PM as a broad-spectrum recognition
tool for pathogenic bacteria.

Based on its strong bacterial recognition and self-aggregation into nanoparticles, D-PM holds great
potential as a vehicle for antibiotic loading and targeted delivery. Pyrene probes, serving as guest
molecules, were readily encapsulated into the internal pockets of nanoparticulate CS, L-PM, and D-PM,
demonstrating their potential as antibiotic carriers (Supplementary Fig. 34). Using hydrophobic
tetracycline (Tet) as a model drug, Tet was successfully encapsulated into the pockets of D-PM to form
Tet-loaded D-PM (T/D-PM)46, which exhibited a uniform size distribution of approximately 180 nm and
well-defined nanostructures (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 35). The drug-loaded T/D-PM delivery system
exhibited a loading capacity of ~ 6.6% and an encapsulation efficiency of ~ 32.9% (Supplementary Fig. 36).
T/D-PM significantly enhanced the antibacterial efficacy of antibiotics, reducing the minimum inhibitory
concentration (MIC) of tetracycline by 4-fold against S. aureus ATCC29213 (Supplementary Table 1).
Moreover, CFU assays further validated that, under the same Tet concentration conditions, T/D-PM
completely eradicated S. aureus, while free Tet, T/CS, and T/L-PM failed to eliminate the bacteria (Fig. 4e).
CLSM images revealed that D-PM improved the internalization of tetracycline through targeted delivery,
showing significantly stronger green fluorescence signals compared to free Tet, T/CS, and T/L-PM (Fig. 4f
and Supplementary Fig. 37a). Targeted antibiotic delivery by D-PM substantially promoted antibacterial
efficacy of antibiotics, as demonstrated by the highest proportion of PI-positive dead bacteria (red, Fig. 4g
and Supplementary Fig. 37b). Notably, T/D-PM potentiated the antibacterial efficacy of tetracycline
against MRSA, halving its MIC and markedly suppressing bacterial colony formation on agar plates
(Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 38).

As expected, tetracycline-containing formulations exhibited no detectable cytotoxicity toward
multiple mammalian cell lines even at concentrations exceeding 40 times the effective antimicrobial dose
(Supplementary Figs. 39 and 40). Additionally, treatment of erythrocytes collected from BALB/c mice with
these formulations at the high concentration revealed no hemolysis, demonstrating excellent
hemocompatibility (Supplementary Fig. 41). The combination of high-efficiency targeted delivery and
favorable biocompatibility underscores the potential of chiral-specific D-peptidoglycan mimics as
promising carriers for biomedical applications.

D-PM intervene wound bacterial infections
The robust incorporation into bacterial metabolism, high-efficiency bacterial recognition, and potential
for bacteria diagnosis and therapy of D-PM prompted further investigation of their efficacy in vivo. FITC-
labeled D-PM effectively marked nearly all S. aureus, which were used to infect wounds (~ 80 mm²) on
the dorsal skin of BALB/c mice with a bacterial load of 1.0 × 106 CFU ml⁻¹ per mouse (Fig. 5a). Following
bacterial infection, the wounds were treated with Cy5-labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM, respectively. After an
additional 4 h, wound tissues were excised, cryosectioned, and visualized using CLSM. As illustrated in Fig.
5b, red fluorescence from D-PM exhibited prominent co-localization with the green fluorescence of S.
aureus, verifying their targeted association. In contrast, no significant red fluorescence was observed in
the CS- or L-PM-treated groups, and uninfected wounds also exhibited no fluorescence signal from D-PM.
Semi-quantitative analysis of co-localization rates demonstrated that D-PM selectively traced a
substantial number of pathogens, a capability absent in CS- and L-PM-treated groups (Supplementary Fig.
42). Moreover, their facile conjugation enables the incorporation of diverse imaging probes into D-PM,
potentially allowing for multimodal diagnostics.

To assess the targeted delivery capabilities of D-PM, a wound infection model was established by
inoculating BALB/c mice with a suspension of S. aureus (1.0 × 10⁶ CFU) for 4 h (Fig. 5c). Infected mice were
treated with PBS (control), free Tet, T/CS, T/L-PM, or T/D-PM, at a dosage of 10 mg Tet per kg of body
weight. Plate counting analysis demonstrated that T/D-PM exhibited the most effective antibacterial
performance in infected wounds, attributable to its targeted antibiotic delivery. As illustrated in Fig. 5d,
T/D-PM markedly enhanced the antibacterial efficacy of tetracycline, nearly eradicating all bacteria within
the wound area. In contrast, T/TCS and T/L-PM treatments failed to improve the antibacterial activity of
tetracycline (Fig. 5e). Gram staining of wound tissue sections further corroborated these findings, showing
that T/D-PM eliminated bacteria from the wound tissues, whereas abundant purple bacteria persisted in
the wounds of other treatment groups (Fig. 5f).

At the end of the observation period, T/D-PM exhibited the greatest efficacy in promoting infected
wound healing, as evidenced by the smallest wound area (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. 43). Hematoxylin
and eosin (H&E) staining revealed that T/D-PM treatment promoted the formation of a thicker dermal
layer in the infected wounds, underscoring its superior antibacterial efficacy compared to free Tet, T/CS,
and T/L-PM (Supplementary Figs. 44 and 45). Masson staining further indicated enhanced collagen
deposition in the T/D-PM group, suggesting accelerated repair of the infected wounds (Fig. 5h,
Supplementary Figs. 46 and 47). Picrosirius red staining revealed that the proportion of type I collagen
relative to the total collagen was increased in the wound tissue of T/D-PM-treated wounds, suggesting
enhanced replacement of type III collagen by type I collagen to promote more effective wound healing
(Supplementary Figs. 48 and 49). Moreover, the infected wounds treated with T/D-PM exhibited elevated
CD31 expression relative to other groups, indicative of increased capillary formation with mature vascular
structures (Supplementary Figs. 50 and 51). The enhanced healing observed in infected wounds treated
with T/D-PM is primarily attributable to its potent antibacterial activity, whereas evaluation in non-
infected wound models further revealed that both D-PM and T/D-PM possessed intrinsic bioactivity that
promotes wound repair (Supplementary Fig. 52). Collectively, these findings highlight that T/D-PM not
only enhances the in vivo antibacterial potency of tetracycline but also facilitates wound healing through
promoting dermal regeneration, collagen deposition, and neovascularization.

D-PM manage systemic bacterial infection
Systemic bacterial infections, such as peritonitis, present a rigorous model to evaluate the targeted
bacterial recognition capability of D-PM under disseminated infection conditions. This model leverages
the highly specific integration of D-PM into bacterial metabolic pathways. To explore this, a bacterial
peritonitis model was established through the intraperitoneal injection of S. aureus ATCC29213 (2.5 × 10⁷
CFU) into the right lower abdomen of BALB/c mice (Fig. 6a). One hour post-infection, fluorescence CS, L-
PM, and D-PM were intraperitoneally administered into the left lower abdomen of the infected mice,
respectively. An in vivo imaging system provided a visual representation of the biomacromolecule
distribution within the body. As the observation time extended, fluorescence signals from CS and L-PM
gradually diminished, becoming almost undetectable by 4 h (Fig. 6b). In contrast, fluorescence signals
from D-PM remained stable even at 4 h post-administration and demonstrated site-specific accumulation
in the peritonitis mice. On the other hand, fluorescence signals of D-PM also decreased in uninfected mice
within 4 h, attributable to the absence of bacterial infections. Semi-quantitative analysis of whole-body
fluorescence, based on average radiant efficiency, demonstrated the progressive clearance of both CS and
L-PM from peritonitis mice, as reflected by the time-dependent attenuation of fluorescence signals (Fig.
6c). In contrast, D-PM demonstrated prolonged retention in peritonitis mice, with fluorescence intensities
approximately 3-fold higher than those of CS and L-PM. However, the signal decay of D-PM in uninfected
mice followed a similar pattern to that of CS and L-PM in bacterial peritonitis models. This infection-
dependent retention of D-PM is primarily due to the efficient incorporation into bacterial metabolic
pathways linked to cell wall biosynthesis, whereas no appreciable D-PM retention is observed in
uninfected mice.

Next, we sought to investigate the bacterial targeting ability of D-PM at the organ level, given that
peritonitis often leads to multiorgan infections. As shown in Fig. 6d, ex vivo imaging revealed pronounced
accumulations of D-PM in non-metabolic organs, specifically the spleens and lungs, distinguishing from
low fluorescence signals in the CS- and L-PM-treated groups. Plate counting revealed comparable bacterial
loads in the spleens and lungs of all peritonitis mice (Supplementary Fig. 53). However, D-PM exhibited
selective enrichment in these infected organs compared to the control, CS-, and L-PM-treated groups.
Notably, uninfected organs showed no obvious D-PM accumulation, highlighting the specificity of
bacterial tracing (Fig. 6e,f). Frozen sections of spleen and lung tissues were analyzed to investigate the
tissue distribution of D-PM within infected organs (Fig. 6g and Supplementary Figs. 54 and 55). A
significantly higher density of fluorescence signal spots was observed in the D-PM-treated group
compared to the L-PM group. The semi-quantitative analysis confirmed that the fluorescence intensity in
the D-PM-treated sections was substantially greater than that of the L-PM-treated group. These findings,
spanning from the systemic level to the organ level, consistently highlight the robust bacterial targeting
capabilities of D-PM, characterized by enhanced retention in infected mice and selective accumulation
within infected organs.

Beyond the ability to target and track bacteria, D-PM holds potential as a therapeutic carrier for
systemic bacterial infections. Following establishment of the S. aureus ATCC29213 peritonitis model,
antibacterial treatment was administered using the different antibiotic delivery systems (Fig. 6h). As
shown in Fig. 6i, the bacterial colony count in ascitic fluid was undetectable in the T/D-PM-treated group,
which was markedly lower than that observed in the control group (4.5 × 103 CFU ml⁻¹), the free Tet-
treated group (1.0 × 103 CFU ml⁻¹), the T/CS-treated group (2.2 × 102 CFU ml⁻¹), and the T/L-PM-treated
group (2.8 × 102 CFU ml⁻¹). Meanwhile, T/D-PM exhibited the highest antibacterial efficacy, effectively
eradicating bacteria in organs, including the spleens and lungs (Fig. 6j,k). Furthermore, T/D-PM exhibited
broad-spectrum and potent antibacterial activity in vivo, demonstrating robust therapeutic efficacy in
murine peritonitis models challenged with antibiotic-resistant S. aureus ATCC43300 (MRSA,
Supplementary Fig. 56) or the Gram-negative pathogen E. coli ATCC25922 (Supplementary Fig. 57). These
findings highlight the potential of D-PM as a drug delivery platform to enhance antibiotic efficacy and
mitigate bacterial resistance.

Last but most importantly, we conducted a comprehensive in vivo safety evaluation of D-PM, which
is critical for its future clinical translation. D-PM was administered intraperitoneally to female BALB/c mice
at doses of 200 or 500 mg per kg body weight twice on day 1, followed by a 7-day observation period
(Supplementary Fig. 58a). No significant changes in body weight were observed throughout the study
(Supplementary Fig. 58b). On day 7, complete blood counts in D-PM-treated mice remained within normal
ranges compared with control groups (Supplementary Fig. 59). Consistently, total plasma immunoglobulin
G (IgG) levels and plasma biochemistry indicators, including alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate
aminotransferase (AST), and blood urea nitrogen (BUN), showed no abnormal alterations (Supplementary
Figs. 60 and 61). Moreover, H&E histological examination of major organs, including the heart, liver,
spleen, lungs, and kidneys, revealed no apparent pathological lesions (Supplementary Fig. 62). Collectively,
these results demonstrate that D-PM exhibits excellent in vivo biocompatibility, even at doses exceeding
those required for bacterial recognition and antibiotic-targeted delivery.

## Methods

Bacterial strains and culture conditions
The bacterial strains utilized in this study are detailed in Supplementary Table 3. The strains were revived
from glycerol stocks and stored at -80 °C until further use. For liquid culture, bacterial strains were
cultured in tryptic soy broth (TSB) or Luria–Bertani broth (LB) at 37 °C with continuous shaking at 220 rpm.
For solid culture, bacteria were plated on LB agar or mannitol salt agar plates and incubated at 37 °C.

Synthesis and characterization of peptidoglycan mimics
Synthesis of chiral peptidoglycan mimics. Chiral peptidoglycan mimics (D-PM and L-PM) were synthesized
as follows: 200.0 mg of chitosans (CS, Mw ≈ 5,000 Da) and 94.6 mg of Boc-D-Ala, combined with 191.2 mg
of 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC.HCl), 115.6 mg of N-
hydroxysuccinimide (NHS), and 384.0 μl of N,N-diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA), were dissolved in a 3:7
(v/v) mixture of dimethylformamide (DMF) and H O solution. The reaction was stirred for 48 h at room
2
temperature. Afterward, the solvent was removed, and the residue was purified by washing 3 times with
methanol and dichloromethane. This step yielded Boc-protected D-PM. To deprotect the Boc group of D-
Ala, trifluoroacetic acid (TFA, 1.0 ml) was added to the Boc-protected D-PM, and the mixture was stirred
for 6 h. The TFA was evaporated under reduced pressure, and the resultant residue was precipitated in
anhydrous diethyl ether. The D-PM product was obtained as a yellow solid (yield: 61.2%). The synthesis
of L-PM was performed under identical conditions, yielding a yellow solid (yield: 58.9%).

Characterizations of peptidoglycan mimics. To confirm the modification of chiral Ala, 1H NMR spectra of
Boc-protected L-PM or Boc-protected D-PM were recorded on a Bruker Avance III 400 MHz spectrometer
in D O, with a sample concentration of 5 mg ml-1. The modification rate of chiral Ala was calculated based
2
on the integral areas of the proton signals corresponding to the sugar rings (δ 3.94–3.10, 5H) and the
methyl group of Ala (-CH₃, δ 1.32–1.26, 3H). The modification rate of chiral Ala was also determined using
the amine titration method. Fluorescamine—a reagent for detecting primary amines—was employed to
assess the amine content in Boc-protected L-PM and Boc-protected D-PM. The fluorescamine solution
was prepared in DMSO at a concentration of 1 mg ml-1, containing 2% DIPEA. CS were used to construct a
standard curve with concentrations ranging from 0 to 200 μg ml-1 on a 96-well microplate. Fluorescence
measurements were taken using a plate reader (SpectraMax M2, Molecular Devices), with excitation at
402 nm and emission at 470 nm. The modification rate of Boc-protected L-PM and Boc-protected D-PM
was then calculated based on the standard curve.

Zeta potentials and nanostructures. The zeta potential and size distribution of CS, L-PM, and D-PM were
measured using a Zetasizer Nano (ZSE, Malvern Panalytical) at a concentration of 400 μg ml-1. The
nanostructures of CS, L-PM, and D-PM were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-
2100Plus, JEOL) after staining with phosphotungstic acid.

Circular dichroism (CD) measurements. CD spectra were conducted for CS, L-PM, and D-PM at a
concentration of 0.5 mg ml-1 in aqueous solutions using a CD spectrometer (J-1500, Jasco). The
measurement parameters included a data pitch of 0.1 nm, a scanning rate of 100 nm min-1, a bandwidth
of 1.00 nm, and a wavelength range from 190 to 260 nm.

Fluorescent PM constructions. Peptidoglycan mimics possess abundant amino groups, making them
suitable for bioconjugation with fluorescent molecules such as FITC, TAMRA, and Cy5, which facilitates
the development of imaging probes. To construct fluorescent D-PM, 20.0 mg of D-PM was dissolved in 1
ml of water, and the pH was adjusted to 8.0 using 1 M NaOH. The fluorescent molecule solution was added
dropwise to the D-PM solution, and the reaction was stirred in the dark for 12 h. The resulting fluorescent
D-PM was purified by dialysis (MWCO 2,000) in water, followed by freeze-drying. The preparation of
fluorescent CS and fluorescent L-PM was carried out using the same procedure. To ensure uniform
fluorescence intensity across the experimental groups, unlabeled PM solutions of equivalent
concentration were used to adjust and standardize the fluorescence intensities. Fluorescent PM labeled
with FITC, TAMRA, and Cy5 were excited at wavelengths of 488 nm, 544 nm, and 637 nm, respectively.
Emission spectra were collected between 460 and 760 nm. The fluorescent stability of FITC-labeled CS,
FITC-labeled L-PM, and FITC-labeled D-PM was assessed at a concentration of 0.02 mg ml-1 in an aqueous
solution. The samples were incubated in the dark at room temperature for different time points.
Fluorescence intensity was measured using a plate reader, with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and
an emission wavelength of 520 nm.

Bacterial recognition ability and mechanisms
Flow cytometry assays. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 were harvested and resuspended in 10
mM PBS to achieve an optical density at 595 nm (OD ) of 0.3. The bacteria were incubated with FITC-
595
labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM at specific concentrations for designated periods. Following incubation, the
bacteria were collected by centrifugation at ~9,000 g for 5 min at 4 °C, washed, and resuspended in 10
mM PBS. The treated bacteria were subsequently analyzed using flow cytometry (CytoFLEX, Beckman
Coulter). The bacterial recognition of chiral PM was assessed using the same treatment protocols for all
pathogenic Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. All representative gating strategies are shown in
Supplementary Fig. 63.

CLSM observation. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 were harvested and resuspended in 10 mM
PBS to achieve an OD of 0.3. The S. aureus was incubated with FITC-labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM at a
595
concentration of 0.5 mg ml-1 for 1 h. After washing off unbound fluorescent PM, the bacterial nuclei were
stained with a 1 μg ml-1 Hoechst 33342 solution for 15 min. The fluorescence signals of the fluorescent
PM located with the bacteria were observed using CLSM (Stellaris 5, Leica).

MST assays. The binding affinity of CS, L-PM, and D-PM to S. aureus ATCC29213 was determined using
MST (Monolith NT.115, NanoTemper). S. aureus (OD = 1.0) was stained with 10 μg ml-1 FM4-64 dye in
595
10 mM PBS. Serial dilutions of CS, L-PM, and D-PM were prepared to create a concentration gradient and
incubated with S. aureus for 10 min at room temperature. The mixtures were loaded into capillaries, and
MST measurements were conducted and analyzed using Nanotemper Analysis software.

UPLC-MS assays. To investigate the effect of D-PM on cell wall biosynthesis, vancomycin was used as a
positive control based on the accumulation of UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide in cultures. Exponential-phase
S. aureus ATCC29213 (OD = 0.3) grown in TSB was pretreated with 130 μg ml-1 chloramphenicol for 15
595
min at 37 °C. Subsequently, 1 mg ml-1 of CS, L-PM, and D-PM, along with 10 μg ml-1 vancomycin, were
added to the S. aureus cultures. After 1-h incubation, the S. aureus was harvested, and the pellets were
resuspended in 500 μl of aqueous solution. The cell suspension was boiled for 30 min and then centrifuged
at ~14,000 g for 15 min. The supernatant was analyzed using UPLC-MS (Orbitrap Exploris 120, Thermo),
and the data were analyzed by FreeStyle (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Xcalibur Version 4.2). By inputting the
chemical formula of UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide into FreeStyle, the targeted molecular weight of
1,149.3516 was used to capture the molecular signal in UPLC-MS results.

To reveal the mechanism of D-PM intervention in synthesis, biosynthetic intermediates of GlcN-D-
Ala-D-Ala and GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala-L-Lys-D-iGlu-L-Ala-MurNAc were tracked and studied. S. aureus (OD =
595
0.3) was treated with CS, L-PM, or D-PM. The supernatant was then analyzed by UPLC-MS to detect and
analyze the molecular signals of GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala (Mw = 321.1536) and GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala-L-Lys-D-iGlu-L-
Ala-MurNAc (Mw = 924.4288).

Molecular docking and dynamics simulation. Molecular docking studies were conducted to predict the
binding interactions between peptidoglycan mimics and key proteins involved in peptidoglycan
biosynthesis, specifically Ddl and MurF. The three-dimensional structures of these proteins were obtained
using AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, and docking simulations were performed using AutoDock
Vina 1.2.3. The docking scores were computed using the built-in scoring functions of AutoDock Vina, which
evaluate binding affinities by considering intermolecular interactions. Following the docking procedure,
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out with GROMACS 2023.2, employing the
CHARMM36m force field and the TIP3P water model. The force field parameters for D-Ala, D-Ala-D-Ala,
GlcN-D-Ala, and GlcN-D-Ala-D-Ala were generated using CGenFF. Hydrogen bonds were constrained using
the LINCS algorithm, with an integration step of 2 fs, and nonbonded interactions were truncated at 12 Å.
The resulting data were visualized using PyMOL 3.0.4.

Biosynthetic inhibition. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 (OD = 0.3) was resuspended in TSB
595
and pretreated with bacterial biosynthetic inhibitors, including Dcy (a D-Ala-D-Ala ligase inhibitor), Amo
(penicillin-binding protein transpeptidase inhibitor), Mer (penicillin-binding protein transpeptidase
inhibitor), Tet (a protein synthesis inhibitor), and Cip (a DNA synthesis inhibitor), all at a concentration of
100 μg ml-1 for 2.5 h. After the removal of the inhibitors, the pretreated S. aureus (OD = 0.3) was
595
incubated with 0.5 mg ml-1 FITC-labeled D-PM in 10 mM PBS for 1 h to analyze bacterial recognition using
flow cytometry. The un-pretreated group served as a positive control, allowing for a comparison of
bacterial recognition in the presence of each inhibitor.

D-PM accumulation in bacterial biosynthesis
Chirality-dependent bacterial accumulation. The accumulation of fluorescent peptidoglycan mimics in
bacteria was detected after multiple rounds of incubation with peptidoglycan mimics. Exponential-phase
S. aureus ATCC29213 (OD = 0.003) was collected and resuspended in an LB medium. After incubation
595
with FITC-labeled L-PM or FITC-labeled D-PM at a concentration of 0.5 mg ml-1 for 1 h, unbound L-PM and
D-PM were removed by washing, yielding Passage 1 (P1) S. aureus. P1 S. aureus was then subjected to a
second incubation with FITC-labeled L-PM or FITC-labeled D-PM for 1 h, followed by washing to remove
unbound PM, resulting in P2 S. aureus. This process was repeated to obtain P3 S. aureus. The accumulation
of chiral PM into each passage of S. aureus biosynthesis was quantified by flow cytometry. Exponential-
phase S. aureus ATCC29213 were harvested and diluted in PBS to an OD of 0.3. The bacterial
595
suspensions were then incubated with CS, L-PM, or D-PM at a concentration of 0.5 mg ml-1 for 1 h. After
incubation, the zeta potential of each sample was measured using a Zetasizer Nano instrument.

3D-SIM for PM hierarchical accumulation. Super-resolution 3D-SIM (N-SIM S, Nikon) was utilized to
visualize the hierarchical incorporation of D-PM into the bacterial cell wall biosynthesis. The bacterial
incubation and treatment protocols were consistent with those described in the flow cytometry assay for
studying chirality-dependent bacterial accumulation. To observe the hierarchical accumulation of PM into
the bacterial cell wall, P1 S. aureus ATCC29213 was derived from incubation with Cy5-labeled L-PM or
Cy5-labeled D-PM, and P2 S. aureus was observed following incubation with TAMRA-labeled L-PM or
TAMRA-labeled D-PM, and P3 S. aureus was examined after incubation with FITC-labeled L-PM or FITC-
labeled D-PM. Each passage of S. aureus (P1, P2, and P3) was observed using 3D-SIM to assess the
hierarchical accumulation of PM into the bacterial cell wall.

SEM for morphology observation. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 was incubated with CS, L-PM,
or D-PM for three consecutive passages to assess morphological alterations. Following treatment, the
bacteria were thoroughly rinsed with PBS and sequentially dehydrated in a graded series of ethanol
solutions. After dehydration, the samples were air-dried and sputter-coated with gold to enhance
conductivity. The bacterial surface morphology was then observed using SEM (MIRA4 LMH, Tescan).

Propidium iodide (PI) influx assay. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 (OD = 0.003) was harvested
595
and resuspended in LB medium. The bacterial suspension was incubated with CS, L-PM, or D-PM at
0.5 mg ml⁻¹ over three consecutive passages. Following treatment, bacteria were stained with 10 μg ml⁻¹
PI for 15 min in the dark, and fluorescence signals were quantified by flow cytometry.

CFU count assays. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 was diluted in PBS to a final concentration of
5 × 10⁵ CFU ml⁻¹. The bacterial suspension was incubated with CS, L-PM, or D-PM at a concentration of 1
mg ml⁻¹ for 1 h to generate Passage 1 (P1). A 10 μl aliquot from each suspension was plated onto mannitol
salt agar. P1 bacteria were then subjected to a second round of incubation with the same materials under
identical conditions for 1 h to obtain Passage 2 (P2), followed by plating of a 10 μl aliquot. This incubation–
plating cycle was repeated once more to generate Passage 3 (P3). All agar plates were incubated at 37 °C
overnight, after which colony-forming units (CFUs) were enumerated.

Targeted delivery systems based on D-PM
Differentiation of bacteria and mammalian cells. NIH 3T3 fibroblasts and S. aureus ATCC29213 were co-
cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS).
FITC-labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM (0.5 mg ml-1, equal fluorescence intensity) were added to the co-culture
system and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. For flow cytometry, unbound fluorescent macromolecules were
removed by washing with PBS. S. aureus was collected by centrifugation, and NIH 3T3 cells were
enzymatically detached using 0.25% trypsin. For CLSM imaging, NIH 3T3 cells and S. aureus were stained
with Hoechst 33342 (1 μg ml-1) for 10 min after removing unbound macromolecules.

Preparation of Tet-loaded D-PM. Tet (20 mg ml-1 in 50 μl DMSO) was mixed with D-PM (20 mg ml-1 in 250
μl water) and sonicated in a water bath. The mixture was then added dropwise into 700 μl water under
ultrasonic conditions, obtaining nanoparticulate Tet-loaded D-PM (T/D-PM). Unencapsulated Tet and
residual organic solvents were removed by dialysis (MWCO: 2,000 Da) against distilled water for 24 h. And
the solution was freeze-dried to obtain the final T/D-PM formulation. Other formulations, including T/CS
and T/L-PM, were prepared using the same procedure. Encapsulation efficiency and drug loading content
were quantified by UV–Vis spectrophotometry (UV-1280, Shimadzu) at 360 nm, based on a standard curve
generated from known Tet concentrations. Pyrene was used as a fluorescent probe to evaluate the
loading capacity of D-PM for guest molecules. Particle size distribution and zeta potential were measured
by Zetasizer Nano. The nanostructure of T/D-PM was visualized using TEM.

Antibacterial activity of T/D-PM. The minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) of free Tet, T/CS, T/L-PM,
and T/D-PM were determined using the standard broth microdilution method following Clinical and
Laboratory Standards Institute guidelines. The exponential-phase bacteria were diluted in fresh TSB to a
final concentration of 5 × 10⁵ CFU ml-1 to prepare the working suspension. A 100 μl aliquot was added to
each well of a 96-well plate. Free Tet, T/CS, T/L-PM, or T/D-PM were then added to the first row at
designated initial concentrations (final volume: 200 μl), followed by a series of 2-fold serial dilutions across
the plate. After incubation at 37 °C for 24 h, the MIC was defined as the lowest antibiotic concentration
that completely inhibited visible bacterial growth. To further evaluate bactericidal activity, PI staining and
CFU assays were conducted. Exponential-phase S. aureus cultures were diluted to OD = 0.3 in PBS and
595
treated with each formulation containing Tet at a final concentration of 2 μg ml-1 for 1 h at 37 °C. Following
treatment, bacterial suspensions were incubated with PI (10 μg ml-1) for 15 min in the dark, followed by
CLSM to visualize PI-positive (dead) bacteria. For CFU assays, exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 and
ATCC43300 were diluted in PBS to 5 × 10⁵ CFU ml⁻¹. S. aureus ATCC29213 was incubated with free Tet,
T/CS, T/L-PM, or T/D-PM (equivalent to 2 μg ml⁻¹ Tet) for 1 h, while S. aureus ATCC43300 was treated with
the same formulations at 0.25 μg ml⁻¹ Tet for 2 h. Each suspension (10 μl aliquot) was plated onto mannitol
salt agar, and CFUs were enumerated after overnight incubation at 37 °C.

Bacterial internalization of T/D-PM. Exponential-phase S. aureus ATCC29213 (OD = 0.3) was treated
595
with different formulations (equivalent to 2 μg ml-1 Tet) for 1 h. After treatment, S. aureus was stained
with Hoechst 33342 (1 μg ml-1, 15 min) to visualize nucleic acids. The intracellular localization of Tet was
examined by CLSM using excitation at 488 nm to detect the intrinsic fluorescence of Tet.

Animal study
All animal experiments were approved by the Laboratory Animal Ethics Committee of Hunan University
(SYXK(XIANG)2018-0006). Ethical guidelines related to animal experiments were strictly followed. Animals
were housed in a controlled environment with a temperature of 20–26 °C, humidity of 40–70%, and a 12
h light/dark cycle.

D-PM for local infection imaging and treatment. Following anesthesia, circular full-thickness wounds
(~80 mm²) were created on the dorsal skin of female BALB/c mice (6–8 weeks old), followed by inoculation
with FITC-D-PM-labeled S. aureus ATCC29213 (1 × 10⁶ CFU). The infected mice were subsequently treated
topically at the wound site with PBS or Cy5-labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM (1 mg per kg body weight). After
4 h, wound tissues were collected, embedded, cryosectioned (~ 10 μm), and stained with Hoechst 33342
for CLSM analysis. Uninfected mice also received Cy5-labeled D-PM as a control. The Pearson’s correlation
coefficient (r) for the colocalization between bacteria (green) and peptidoglycan mimics (red) was
quantified using Fiji/ImageJ (version 1.54f).

For antibacterial efficacy evaluation, the same wound infection model was employed. After 4 h of
infection, the mice were treated with PBS, free Tet, T/CS, T/L-PM, and T/D-PM at a dosage of 10 mg Tet
per kg of body weight. Treatments were administered topically every 12 h for a total of 2 doses.
Throughout the treatment period, the wound area and the body weight of infected mice were closely
monitored. At designated time points, the infection wounds were swabbed under sterile conditions, and
the bacteria were suspended in PBS and plated on mannitol salt agar for CFU enumeration. Following
euthanasia, wound tissues were fixed in 4% polyformaldehyde, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned for
histological analysis. Gram staining assessed bacterial burden, while the stainings by H&E, Masson,
picrosirius red and CD31 immunofluorescence were performed to evaluate tissue regeneration and
neovascularization.

D-PM for systemic infection imaging and treatment. A mouse peritonitis model (female BALB/c) was
established by intraperitoneal injection of S. aureus ATCC29213 (2.5 × 10⁷ CFU in 100 μl PBS) into the right
side of the abdomen. After 1 h of infection, Cy5-labeled CS, L-PM, or D-PM (5 mg Tet per kg body weight)
were administered intraperitoneally into the left side of the abdomen. Control animals received the
treatment with Cy5-labeled D-PM in the absence of infection. In vivo imaging was conducted at 10 min, 1
h, 2 h, and 4 h post-administration using an in vivo imaging system (IVIS Spectrum CT, PerkinElmer). Major
organs were harvested and subjected to ex vivo fluorescence imaging. Fluorescence intensity was
quantified using Living Image software. Bacterial burdens in tissues were determined by plating tissue
homogenates on mannitol salt agar. These tissues were embedded, cryosectioned, and mounted as
described for wound samples, followed by CLSM imaging to assess the tissue distribution of Cy5-labeled
CS, L-PM, or D-PM.

For antibacterial efficacy assessment, female BALB/c mice were intraperitoneally inoculated with
100 μl of bacterial suspension containing S. aureus ATCC29213 (2.5 × 10⁷ CFU), S. aureus ATCC43300
(MRSA, 2.5 × 10⁷ CFU), or E. coli ATCC25922 (1.0 × 10⁷ CFU) in PBS. After 1 h, mice were treated with PBS,
free Tet, T/CS, T/L-PM, or T/D-PM. The administered dose was 10 mg Tet per kg body weight for S. aureus
ATCC29213 and MRSA ATCC43300 infections, and 20 mg Tet per kg body weight for E. coli ATCC25922
infection, delivered intraperitoneally every 12 h for a total of two doses. After 24 h of the first treatment,
mice were euthanized, and ascitic fluid, along with major organs, were aseptically collected. Samples were
homogenized, serially diluted, and plated on agar for CFU enumeration.

Safety evaluation of D-PM. D-PM suspended in PBS was administered intraperitoneally to female BALB/c
mice at 200 or 500 mg D-PM per kg body weight, with PBS alone serving as the control. Body weights were
recorded daily throughout the study. On day 7 post-administration, whole blood and plasma were
collected for routine hematological analysis and plasma biochemical profiling, including
immunoglobulin G (IgG), alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), and blood urea
nitrogen (BUN). Mice were then euthanized, and major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys)
were excised, fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned for
hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and histological examination.

Statistical information
Statistical significance between two groups was assessed using a two-tailed unpaired t-test. All
experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. Data are presented as
mean ± s.d. Differences were considered statistically significant at P < 0.05 (*P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; ***P <
0.001; ****P < 0.0001); P > 0.05 was considered not significant (NS).
